newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices turn lower as Iraq calls ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices turn lower as Iraq calls ceasefire.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices fell after Iraq called a ceasefire Friday, reversing a rally to near post-Gulf War highs on jitters about U.S. military stikes to punish the country for raids on Kurdish rebels.

On the New York Mercantile Exchange, October crude oil fell 60 cents to $24.40 at around 2 p.m. EDT, after the Iraqi News Agency reported that Iraq would halt its attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes flying over its north and south.

An official spokesman for the ruling Revolutionary Command Council told the agency the ceasefire was a response to an initiative by the Russian leadership and nations friendly to Iraq which denounced U.S. missile strikes on the country.
"That's definitely bearish news," said ARB Oil Managing Director Gerald Samuels.
In response to the Iraqi report, the White House said it will judge Baghdad on it actions and not on its statements.

Crude oil had risen as high as $25.35 earlier, flirting with the post-Gulf war high of $25.70 a barrel set April 16. It was the highest level reached since the 1991 U.S.-led Gulf War, when allied forces launched an attack on Iraq to liberate Kuwait.
World oil prices have risen about $2 a barrel since the U.S.-Iraq tensions started two weeks ago.
Refined product prices also turned downward. October heating oil fell 87 cents to 68.30 cents a gallon. October gasoline slid 111 cents to 64.80 cents a gallon.
"We have to put this in perspective. Crude was up $3.00 since this thing started," said John Saucer, a Smith Barney analyst.
"We could see more selling. We had stalled after making highs in the morning, and there was no follow-through."
Saucer said the price of October crude could stay between $24.50 and $25.00, as Friday's options expiration of October crude could keep the price near the strikes.
